power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Motor dysfunction is a major contributor to disability in pediatric-onset monogenic neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), yet systematic quantifications of motor phenotypes across development using validated clinical scales remain underdeveloped.
Existing studies have classified motor phenotypes rather than quantified domain-specific severity, limiting their use as outcome measures in clinical trials.
Here, we systematically quantify motor dysfunction using established clinical rating scales to explore their utility as motor endpoints.

In this cross-sectional observational study, 102 individuals with NDDs (0.5-38 years) secondary to pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in five genes (SCN2A, KCNQ2, CSNK2A1, CACNA1A, SCN8A) and 31 unaffected sibling controls underwent standardized motor assessments using the Scale for Assessment and Rating of Ataxia, Burke-Fahn-Marsden Dystonia Scale, and the Modified Ashworth Scale.
Regional and functional categorization of parameters enabled differentiated interpretation.
Gene-specific patterns were evaluated using z-score standardization across the pooled affected cohort, with gene-level averaging and nonparametric bootstrap-derived 95% confidence intervals.
Dysfunction was present in individuals with NDDs across speech (90%), coordination (87%), dystonia (83.3%), gross motor (82.4%) and spasticity (42.2%), with minimal impairment in controls (0-12.9%).

We observed substantial heterogeneity across motor domains and subdomains; ataxic dysarthria had the highest score distribution (median 0.83 [IQR, 0.17-1.0]), whereas spasticity showed near-floor scores.

Individuals with SCN2A variants demonstrated higher mean z-scores across multiple subdomains than other genes, with more consistent deviations observed in coordination and speech domains (Coordination: mean z = 0.29, 95% CI 0.03-0.54; Speech: mean z = 0.3, 95% CI 0.03-0.57), whereas domain-specific or less pronounced patterns were observed in other genes.
The ataxia and dystonia scales demonstrated low floor and ceiling effects.

Discussion: Using three clinical scales across a broad developmental and functional range, our study moves motor phenotyping in monogenic NDDs from categorical description toward quantitative, domain-resolved severity assessment.
Exploratory analysis indicates marked heterogeneity in severity profiles across genes, most notably in SCN2A, suggesting potential selective motor vulnerability.
These findings provide evidence for the feasibility of motor phenotyping and provide preliminary, cross-sectional benchmark severity distributions.
Subsequent longitudinal validation and validation in larger, longitudinal, and variant-stratified cohorts will enable natural history studies and future therapeutic trials alongside seizure outcomes.

Monogenic neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) are characterized by diverse neurological, cognitive and autonomic impairments. 1, 2 Motor dysfunction, ranging from abnormalities of tone to severe movement disorders, is a commonly observed yet poorly studied feature, despite its substantial impact on long-term functional outcomes and quality of life. [3] [4] [5] Recent evidence suggests motor dysfunction in individuals with NDDs is diverse 6 , present across a broad age range, 7, 8 and associated with most NDD-related genes. 9, 10 Similarly, large repositories of parent-reported data such as Simons Searchlight 11 and metaanalyses 12, 13 provide evidence for the near-universal presence of motor dysfunction in monogenic NDDs, emphasizing that it is not merely a gene-or syndrome-specific feature.

text.text: It is thus imperative to develop tools to reliably detect motor dysfunction and monitor its evolution.
However, the motor outcome measures validated for NDDs remain underdeveloped, especially in contrast to seizure-related outcomes, due to several limitations of our current knowledgebase.

Firstly, motor dysfunction can be subtle in severity and difficult to distinguish from seizures, complicating detection and clinical management. 14 As such, much of the prior work has focused on identification and subtype classification, rather than on quantifying severity. 6 The limited previous application of standardized motor rating scales across a wide age range has further restricted the quantification of motor dysfunction and inclusion of motor outcome measures in clinical trials. 15, 16 Second, monogenic NDDs are rare, constraining prior studies by cohort size.

text.text: To define severity estimates for motor dysfunction in individuals with monogenic NDDs, we quantified motor phenotypes in a large, cross-sectional cohort spanning five monogenic NDDs from infancy through adulthood using established rating scales.
We provide domain-level quantification of motor dysfunction and establish genotype-associated patterns.
By anchoring motor phenotyping to three clinician-assessed scales, this work provides preliminary benchmark distributions of motor dysfunction severity and frequency.
Subsequent longitudinal follow-up studies will evaluate within-person trajectories, test-retest reliability, and responsiveness to clinically meaningful change.
This will support their eventual use as quantitative outcome measures for motor function in therapeutic trials for NDDs. 20

Motor dysfunction is widespread across monogenic NDDs but poorly defined and monitored. 26 In this prospectively recruited, cross-sectional study, we quantify motor dysfunction frequency and severity in 102 individuals with monogenic NDDs using three complementary scales assessing ataxia, spasticity, and dystonia, with particularly deep quantification of individuals with SCN2A, KCNQ2, and CSNK2A1-related NDDs.

text.text: Unlike prior studies utilizing retrospective chart review or video assessment, we utilize a standardized video protocol across five monogenic NDDs with domain-resolved quantification, providing greater phenotypic resolution and measurement rigor than categorical descriptions of motor dysfunction alone.
Although gene-stratified results are exploratory, our observations suggest potential genotype-specific motor profiles that may inform the design of larger, adequately powered studies.
Overall, our results provide crucial benchmark distributions of domainspecific motor dysfunction in monogenic NDDs.
Subsequent longitudinal validation will support the development of motor endpoints for natural history studies and clinical trial readiness in rare diseases.
Prior studies have established the presence of motor dysfunction in individuals with monogenic NDDs.

Van der Veen et al. reported the diversity of movement disorders in 77 individuals covering 38 genetic DEEs with known movement disorders, identifying both hypo-and hyperkinetic disorders using caregiver-submitted and archived clinical videos. 6 Montanucci et al. similarly provide frequency estimates of motor phenotypes in 1210 probands across 87 NDD-associated genes without in-depth quantification. 27 More recently, Bernardi et al summarized the growing body of knowledge suggesting motor dysfunction is prominent in epilepsy-associated NDDs. 28 Gene-specific studies also suggest disease mechanism-dependent motor dysfunction but they primarily describe motor phenotypes as comorbidities rather than quantifying frequencies and genotypeassociated expression patterns. 10, [29] [30] [31] [32] [33] A key retrospective study by Mastrangelo et al. provides important reference ages for motor phenotypes. 34 Thus, the major gap is no longer whether motor dysfunction occurs, but how to measure its severity so that it can be used in natural history studies and trials.

text.text: Our work targets this gap by applying validated, domain-resolved scales across a wide age, building a foundation for systematic motor outcome assessment in NDDs.
Our analyses demonstrate low frequency and lower score distributions of spasticity across the NDD cohort.

Spasticity reflects velocity-dependent hypertonia arising from corticospinal tract injury, classically associated with perinatal brain injury. 35 In monogenic NDDs, focal corticospinal injury is not typically expected or rare, in line with our observation of an overall low spasticity burden.

text.text: Accordingly, the pronounced floor effect observed for the MAS may reflect a genuinely low prevalence of spasticity in this population.
However, given the substantial floor effects across spasticity-related subdomains (70-86%), reduced sensitivity of the scale to detect milder forms of hypertonia cannot be excluded.
These findings should therefore be interpreted cautiously, and spasticity-related results may be influenced by both true low frequency and measurement limitations.

Hypotonia is the most frequently reported motor phenotype across NDDs and developmental and epileptic encephalopathies. 9, 36 We did not systematically measure hypotonia due to the lack of standardized scales applicable across development, but it was clinically apparent in most assessments, and we hypothesize that our data provides indirect evidence for this observation.

text.text: A large proportion of our cohort exhibited dystonia; multiple lines of evidence suggest that hypotonia may predispose to secondary dystonic posturing, particularly of distal extremities. 37 In line with this hypothesis, dystonic features were often discrete and limited to distal extremities, possibly also reflecting abnormal sensory processing, which can contribute to focal dystonia. 38, 39 Together, these factors provide a biological basis for the higher severity of dystonic features and the possible association with widespread hypotonia observed in this cohort.

However, in the absence of validated motor scales applicable across both ambulatory and non-ambulatory individuals, this approach allowed for pragmatic stratification of motor severity across the cohort.
Speech dysfunction was prominent across our cohort, including among individuals with milder limb or axial motor dysfunction.
The SARA speech item assesses the intelligibility of spoken language as a measure of ataxic dysarthria.

However, it has not been validated for individuals who have not acquired speech because of developmental impairment. 25 In these participants, a high score cannot be attributed specifically to ataxic dysarthria and may instead reflect language or cognitive impairment. 40 The pronounced ceiling effect in our cohort may partly reflect this limitation; the item also does not capture vocalizations, gestures, or other forms of communication particularly relevant to cognitively impaired individuals. [41] [42] [43] We therefore interpreted these scores as measures of observed function, not isolated evidence of cerebellar impairment.

However, it also cannot adequately distinguish whether speech impairment is related to cognitive or motor vocalization.
Overall, the value of speech assessment as a functional outcome measure cannot be understated.

text.text: Key drawbacks that must be mentioned are that our cohort may not be representative of all NDDs given its limitation to five genes and the pre-dominance of channelopathy-related genes.
Moreover, the lack of variantlevel stratification within the gene groups may also limit the generalizability of our findings.

For instance, SCN2A variants exhibit substantial functional heterogeneity, with gain-of-function variants typically associated with severe DEE and loss-of-function variants more commonly linked to milder neurodevelopmental phenotypes. 46 Pooling these mechanistically distinct variant classes within a single gene-level group may obscure meaningful differences in motor dysfunction expression and contribute to variability in the observed severity patterns.

text.text: This may partially explain the variability and confidence intervals overlapping zero observed within the SCN2A group.
Accordingly, the gene-level estimates presented here should be interpreted as aggregate patterns rather than mechanism-specific effects.

Future studies incorporating more homogeneous cohorts or stratification by variant-level biology, severity, and age of onset will be necessary to disentangle gene-specific effects from underlying clinical heterogeneity.
Our study has several other limitations that should be considered when interpreting these findings.
First, recruitment from gene-specific advocacy events and a tertiary academic center likely introduce ascertainment bias.
Participation in these settings requires travel and caregiver availability, likely limiting inclusion of individuals with more severe disabilities.
These individuals are also more likely to receive ancillary therapy support, limiting generalizability to individuals without access to these services.
Moreover, increased mortality among individuals with severe NDDs may contribute to an overrepresentation of milder phenotypes in older age groups.
Therefore, age-associated findings should be interpreted cautiously.
Our recruitment sites likely also introduced socioeconomic biases, reflected in the predominantly White cohort which limits external validity to racial and ethnic minorities.

This limitation is common in rare disease research and underscores the need for strategies to improve accessibility and inclusivity across socioeconomic backgrounds. 21 Further collaboration with patient-advocacy groups to address this gap, for instance by promoting virtual, in-person assessments may improve generalizability and access to larger, representative cohorts.

text.text: Previous studies have demonstrated the presence of additional motor phenotypes such as chorea and myoclonus in patients with NDDs. 6, 27 Although we frequently observed these features, they were not systematically analyzed.
text.formatted: Previous studies have demonstrated the presence of additional motor phenotypes such as chorea and myoclonus in patients with NDDs. <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">27</ref> Although we frequently observed these features, they were not systematically analyzed.

text.text: Many of these phenotypes lack standardized severity scales that are broadly applicable across developmental ages.

Our focus on ataxia, dystonia, and spasticity was therefore driven by the availability of validated rating instruments, highlighting the need to develop scalable, quantitative tools to enable inclusion of a wider range of motor phenotypes as outcome measures.
Additionally, motor assessments were scored by a single expert rater, supervised by developmental neurology and movement disorder specialists.
Inter-rater reliability testing between the primary rater and an expert committee demonstrated excellent agreement for the BFMS (ICC(2,1) = 0.90).
However, scales such as the MAS require in-person examination and cannot be reliably scored post-hoc using videos alone, limiting formal assessment of reliability for all scales.
Future studies would benefit from incorporating protocols optimized for remote and asynchronous scoring to facilitate broader participation, and independent validation.
Moreover, we did not systematically collect detailed longitudinal clinical data on potential confounders such as seizure burden, antiseizure medication exposure, or prior neurosurgical interventions.

As many participants were recruited at advocacy conferences, comprehensive medical histories were not uniformly available, and we cannot rule out additional underlying structural brain abnormalities which may influence motor phenotypes and increase unmeasured heterogeneity within the cohort.

Future studies incorporating structured clinical data collection and medication histories will be necessary to disentangle intrinsic genotype-associated motor dysfunction from treatment or comorbidity-related effects.

Finally, we emphasize the limited sample size of our study, which may affect statistical power and generalizability; findings should therefore be interpreted within the context of an exploratory study of rare monogenic NDDs.
In summary, this study provides a much needed standardized, domain-resolved quantification of motor dysfunction across developmental stages in monogenic NDDs.

Our findings demonstrate that motor assessment scales are straightforward to administer and can be reliably applied with appropriate training, making them well suited for routine clinical use and research.
Their broader adoption as standard tools in clinical practice would substantially expand the availability of structured motor data across diverse settings.

This framework establishes a foundation for longitudinal motor phenotyping and supports the development of quantitative motor outcome measures for natural history studies and emerging clinical trials. 47

text.text: The inclusion criterion for individuals with NDDs was the presence of a pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant in the five NDD-associated genes we studied as per American College of Medical Genetics (ACMG) guidelines 48 .
Seizure history was not required for inclusion and was not used to define the analytic cohort.
Individuals with acute illnesses that could interfere with safe participation in the neurological examination were excluded from the study.
Unaffected siblings of enrolled individuals with NDDs were included as controls without prior phenotype matching to facilitate pragmatic recruitment and reduce selection bias.
Gene selection was driven by feasibility of recruitment, including patients evaluated in multidisciplinary clinics and at genespecific advocacy events during the study period.
As such, the cohort represents a pragmatic sample of individuals with monogenic NDDs rather than a biologically uniform group selected for mechanistic similarity.
The only inclusion criterion for controls was no known history of any NDD-associated variants.
However, no explicit genetic testing was performed to rule out any incidental genetic findings.
A formal a priori sample size calculation was not performed due to the rarity and heterogeneity of the studied NDDs.

Recruitment was based on feasibility, and all eligible individuals during the recruitment period were invited to participate; therefore, we emphasize effect sizes and confidence intervals rather than post-hoc power estimates.
All participants and/or legal guardians underwent a written informed consent process prior to study procedures.
Age groups were defined as infancy (0-2 years), early (3-5 years) and late childhood (6-10 years), adolescence (11-18 years) and adulthood (>18 years) (Table 1).

text.text: All consents, identifiable participant information and clinical data were stored in an instance of UTHealth RedCap to ensure strict adherence to data protection regulations.
Each participant was assigned a unique identifier (UID); demographic and clinical data were de-identified prior to extraction from RedCap for analysis.
Motor exam scores were collected in a blinded dataset containing the UID as the only identifier.

The primary inperson rater was not blinded to recruitment context in all cases, whereas post-hoc expert committee BFMS rerating was performed blinded to participant identity, genotype, and clinical information.
Variant pathogenicity (re)classification was performed by variant analysis experts and genetic counselors in the Lal Group following ACMG criteria and using established in silico tools.

We followed the recent variant curation expert panel (VCEP) guidelines developed for epilepsy-associated voltage-gated sodium channels (https://clinicalgenome.org/docs/clingen-variant-curation-expert-panel-vcep-protocol/).

text.text: Assessments took place at UTHealth's UT Physicians Clinic at the Texas Medical Center or in dedicated examination rooms at conference venues.
The rater conducted examinations and team members assisted with documentation.
We utilized two uniquely positioned Sony HDRCX405 Handycam Camcorders to record all standardized assessments for retrospective curation and independent rating for reliability testing.
Caregivers were present throughout to ensure participants' safety and comfort.

Motor phenotypes were quantified using the Scale for the Assessment and Rating of Ataxia (SARA), the Burke-Fahn-Marsden Dystonia Rating Scale (BFMS), and the Modified Ashworth Scale (MAS) for spasticity.
Domains and subdomains were established by stratifying individual parameters into clinically meaningful groups based on body region or motor function (Table 2).
text.formatted: Domains and subdomains were established by stratifying individual parameters into clinically meaningful groups based on body region or motor function (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">2</ref>).

text.text: For non-ambulatory participants, SARA items requiring independent mobility (e.g., gait and stance) were assigned the maximum score, reflecting inability to perform the task.
For pre-ambulatory participants, these items were not scored and were designated as not applicable.

This approach was selected to preserve the ordinal structure of the scale and enable consistent severity categorization across the cohort in the absence of validated measures spanning the full developmental and functional spectrum.

For the BFMS, final scores were calculated by multiplying raw scores with the provocation factor -defined as the presence of a phenotype at rest or only in certain ranges of motion -as described previously. 23

text.text: No imputation of missing data was performed.

Analyses were conducted using an available-case approach, with observations included when the variables required for a given analysis were available to maximize sample size in this observational study.
Consequently, denominators varied across analyses depending on the completeness of the relevant motor assessment.
Composite motor subdomain scores were derived by summing the available component scores within each subdomain, with available-item maximum used for proportion calculations.
Participants for whom all component parameters within a subdomain were unavailable were assigned a missing value for that composite subdomain.
When at least one component parameter was available, the composite score was calculated using the available observations without imputation.

Binary motor phenotypes were classified as present when at least one contributing parameter had a score ≥1 and absent when one or more contributing parameters were observed and all observed parameters had scores of 0.
Binary phenotypes were considered missing only when all contributing parameters were unavailable.
Accordingly, frequency estimates were calculated using the number of participants with available data for each phenotype as the denominator.

For exploratory gene-level analyses, patient-referenced z-scores were calculated only for observations with available motor scores and parameters demonstrating non-zero variability across the affected cohort.
Parameters without measurable variability in the affected cohort were excluded from z-score standardization (Table S4).
text.formatted: Parameters without measurable variability in the affected cohort were excluded from z-score standardization (Table <ref type="table">S4</ref>).

text.text: Inter-rater reliability analyses used only jointly scored items from both raters, and the primary ICC analysis was restricted to assessments with complete paired ratings across all nine BFMS items.
No imputation was performed for missing paired ratings.
The number and proportion of observations excluded because of missing data at each stage of the analysis are summarized in Table S4.
text.formatted: The number and proportion of observations excluded because of missing data at each stage of the analysis are summarized in Table <ref type="table">S4</ref>.

text.text: All motor assessments were scored by a single primary rater (S.B.) with formal training in the use of the SARA, BFMS, and MAS.

Training consisted of supervised scoring of representative videos, scoring guideline review prior to study initiation under direct supervision by two pediatric neurologists (N.T. and G.V.A.) and a physical therapist (S.E.M.) specialized in pediatric movement disorders.
This supervision occurred as part of routine multidisciplinary clinical care.
Participants with incomplete motor examinations due to fatigue, behavioral intolerance, or time constraints were retained in the analysis.
No participants were excluded post-enrollment; individuals unable to participate in motor assessments were not enrolled in the study.
Post-hoc blind, independent re-rating of 59 BFMS assessments was conducted by a movement disorder expert committee (N.T., S.E.M. and R.F).
Inter-rater reliability was evaluated using a two-way random-effects, absoluteagreement, single-measure intraclass correlation coefficient [ICC(2,1)].
Total BFMS scores were calculated using items scored by both raters.
The primary analysis was restricted to assessments with complete paired ratings across all nine BFMS items; two assessments with one missing paired item were excluded.
No imputation was performed.
An available-case sensitivity analysis including all 59 assessments produced nearly identical results.
Statistical analyses were performed in R (v4.4.1) (RStudio v2024.0.2).

For frequency analysis (Figure 1A), participants were classified according to the presence or absence of five broad motor phenotypes (gross motor deficit, coordination deficit, speech deficit, dystonia, and spasticity).
text.formatted: For frequency analysis (Figure <ref type="figure">1A</ref>), participants were classified according to the presence or absence of five broad motor phenotypes (gross motor deficit, coordination deficit, speech deficit, dystonia, and spasticity).

text.text: Sums and percentages were calculated separately for controls and individuals with NDDs.
Differences between groups were evaluated Fisher's exact tests.
P values were adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure.
Motor subdomain severity in individuals with NDDs was summarized by calculating composite subdomain scores and expressing each as a proportion of the maximum possible score (Figure 1B).

text.text: Continuous variables were summarized using medians and interquartile ranges (IQRs).
Floor and ceiling effects for each subdomain (Figure S1) were defined as scores <5% or >95% of the maximum possible score, respectively.

text.text: To characterize gene-level motor phenotype patterns (Figure 2), controls were excluded and individual motor parameter scores were standardized relative to the pooled affected cohort.

text.text: Parameter-level z-scores were averaged within assessments across parameters belonging to the same motor subdomain, followed by aggregation within genotype groups.
Mean z-scores therefore represent the average deviation from the affected-cohort mean.
Uncertainty was estimated using nonparametric bootstrap resampling (2,000 iterations) with percentile-based 95% confidence intervals (Table S3).
